name: Freya Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government, and what you say stays confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Freya Ziegler, 58. After a vocational certificate I joined the electricity company as a junior lineworker, building and repairing power lines. The day begins with checking harnesses and loading the bucket truck, then I work under a lead worker while we isolate a line and change fittings. I like chasing a fault from a dark window back to a burnt connector. I still fumble some hardware and ask for a second check, even though I enjoy learning a new system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a work decision matter at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nils runs a small bread stall three mornings a week, and our children are grown and live elsewhere. We have roughly five months of expenses saved, though stall income jumps around. I use AI every day to turn the manual into practice questions and to compare my own notes, then I confirm the answers with a trainer. I would rather test a new tool myself than guess what it can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a faster form is pleasant but the desk cannot inspect a wire. The pole still waits for us. I would happily use the saved desk time to inspect another connection properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my shift pattern to stay fairly steady. Nils’s stall has bad weather weeks, so our five months of savings feels useful rather than excessive, and I cannot assume a retirement income yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep taking supervised repair shifts and my daily AI practice quiz. This month I’d ask the trainer to review the clearance questions I keep missing; in 2029 I’d put a small extra amount from each regular pay into our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel comfortable with this picture, mostly because I get time to become competent. I still have to earn the trust to work without someone checking each fitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where has your study method failed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once copied the wrong diagram number into my notebook, and the AI quiz repeated it back as if it were true. The trainer caught it before I took the notebook up in the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you put aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nils and I have discussed putting twenty from each pay into a separate savings account. If the stall has a poor month, the amount can pause without touching the rent money.

say: I’d welcome **faster forms** while keeping time for careful line inspection.
I’d tell coworkers **hands-on repairs** remain the main work.
think: I expect my **line shifts** to continue while I learn the trade.
Nils’s **weather-sensitive stall** makes five months saved valuable.
do: Keep **supervised repairs** and review missed clearance questions with the trainer.
Put **twenty per pay** into a separate reserve when stall income allows.
feel: I feel **comfortable with time** to build competence, though I still need checking.
S0.quote: The pole still waits for us.
fieldNote: Freya treats a false quiz answer as a **manual-check lesson**, not proof that every new tool is useless.
Her savings plan is modest and conditional because **bread stall income** varies with weather.

steps.text: Take supervised line repairs and confirm fittings with the lead worker
Review missed AI clearance questions with the trainer
Put twenty from regular pay into a reserve when stall income allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew I want to try a new scheduling tool on a real repair day. I would also ask the supervisor to publish how it handles travel, isolation and testing time before using it to judge anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think office scheduling and ordering will change first, while our hands still do repairs. If the company sends fewer trucks after software cuts wasted journeys, a junior like me could lose paid hours even if the tool works well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d volunteer to compare AI route suggestions with actual truck journeys for a month. In 2029 I’d keep paid line shifts, show the supervisor the missed travel and safety time, and ask to learn how the tool reads our work orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel excited to test a tool and worried about what a smaller roster would mean. I can be keen on the software and still need the shift it might remove.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a route tool miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One repair behind the market requires backing the bucket truck down a narrow lane. A map marks it as a quick stop, but setting the barriers safely takes nearly as long as the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the stall replace lost pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nils could add a market day, but we would not count that as a wage replacement. He would need a good pitch and enough bread sold before we changed our budget.

say: I’d ask to **test scheduling** on actual repair days.
I’d request **published allowances** for travel, isolation and electrical checks.
think: I expect **office tasks** to change before physical line repair.
A smaller **truck roster** could take away my junior hours.
do: Compare **AI route suggestions** with one month of truck journeys.
Keep **paid line shifts** in 2029 and show missed time to the supervisor.
feel: I feel **excited and worried** because useful software could still reduce shifts.
S1.quote: I can be keen on the software and still need the shift it might remove.
fieldNote: Freya volunteers to test **real truck journeys**, fitting her willingness to try new technology early.
Her private concern is a **smaller roster** despite public interest in efficiency, and the bread stall cannot reliably replace wages.

steps.text: Compare AI route suggestions with actual truck journeys for a month
Take paid line shifts and show missed travel time to the supervisor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full thinking AI in 2028 could handle plans and orders, while our crew still climbs until capable robots arrive around 2031. I would ask the company to show real paid posts for people who learn to maintain the new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 at the first date and 63 at the robot date. Five months saved is not enough to stop earning, and a bread stall will not cover our rent if my line shifts vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the training lead to show me any line robot demonstrations and enroll in a funded maintenance course if one exists. In 2029 I’d keep repair shifts and apply for the utility’s equipment trainee opening if posted; before 2031 I’d cut the expensive stall upgrade we were considering until we knew the wage outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel shaken by the short gap, although I would want to see the robot close up. A demonstration is interesting; a paid contract is what keeps our home running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase would you hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nils wants a second oven for the stall, and I usually like trying a bigger market. In this picture I would hold that purchase, because the same savings may need to cover months with no line wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would maintenance last after robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn to replace a robot’s worn part, but a capable robot might eventually do that too. I would ask about the job term and placement, not call maintenance a permanent hiding place.

say: I’d request **real paid posts** linked to equipment training.
I’d explain **2028 planning AI** comes before robots climb around 2031.
think: At **63**, robots could end junior line shifts before I can retire.
Our **five-month reserve** and bread stall cannot replace my wage for long.
do: Seek a **funded maintenance course** if the utility offers one.
Keep **repair shifts** in 2029 and apply for an equipment trainee opening if posted.
Postpone the **second stall oven** until wages are clearer.
feel: I feel **shaken but curious**, aware that a demonstration cannot pay rent.
S2.quote: A demonstration is interesting; a paid contract is what keeps our home running.
fieldNote: Freya pairs technical curiosity with a demand for **paid placement**, rather than treating a robot demonstration as security.
The proposed **second oven** is a concrete investment she would defer to protect household cash.

steps.text: Enroll in funded equipment maintenance if a course place exists
Keep taking paid line repair shifts in 2029
Apply for a posted utility equipment trainee opening
Postpone buying a second oven for Nils’s bread stall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that five years would let us test real equipment and negotiate what happens to the people using it. Thinking AI could take planning in 2031; line robots could follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when plans change and 66 when robots do repairs. I might retire near then, but I have not seen a pension estimate and Nils’s stall income can swing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a pension estimate and ask the trainer for a supervised equipment maintenance day. In 2032 I’d keep line shifts, compare the real maintenance work with my skills, and apply for a funded trainee vacancy if one exists; before 2034 I’d review the numbers with Nils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more capable of choosing with five years in hand. I still know a trial day does not create a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a maintenance trial useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see a broken sensor, not just a polished robot on a display stand. If I can diagnose it alongside a maintainer, I will know what training I actually need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the pension figure change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pension estimate covered our basic bills, Nils and I might plan fewer working days later. If it did not, I would keep applying rather than mark a retirement date on a calendar.

say: I’d ask for **real equipment tests** and worker terms during the five-year warning.
I’d separate **2031 planning** from physical robots around 2034.
think: I may need wages at **66** if retirement figures fall short.
Nils’s **variable stall income** makes the pension estimate important.
do: Request a **pension estimate** and a supervised maintenance day.
Keep **line shifts** in 2032 and apply for a funded trainee vacancy if posted.
feel: I feel **more capable of choosing**, while knowing a trial creates no vacancy.
S3.quote: I still know a trial day does not create a job.
fieldNote: Freya wants to diagnose a **broken sensor** beside a maintainer, a practical test of training needs.
She keeps retirement conditional on **basic bills** and paid work conditional on an actual opening.

steps.text: Request a pension estimate and compare it with basic household bills
Apply for a funded equipment trainee vacancy if posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my friends that ten years is long enough to make several small decisions instead of one desperate jump. Thinking AI could run the records in 2036, with capable line robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 at the second. Perhaps I will have retired before robots take the climb, but I need to know the pension and what the stall can really earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d check the pension statement each year and keep doing safe line repairs as long as my body allows. In 2037 I’d accept paid equipment checks if offered, and Nils and I would decide whether to stop working only after measuring our actual bills against income; if the figures failed, I’d apply for maintenance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel hopeful with that much warning. I also notice how much of my plan depends on a future offer I cannot see today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a camera on your current job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would help test a new inspection camera on a line job if the company trained us and gave us enough time. I could compare the image with what we find on the pole, then decide if it earns my trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nils would like to travel once the stall closes, and I would too. We would put that wish after rent, food and medical costs, not before them.

say: I’d favour **small yearly decisions** during the decade before robots reach repairs.
I’d explain **2036 records** change before line robots around 2039.
think: I might retire before **71**, but the pension and stall earnings are unknown.
A future **equipment offer** cannot be counted as income today.
do: Check the **pension statement** each year while keeping safe repairs.
Take **paid equipment checks** in 2037 if offered.
Apply for **maintenance work** if retirement figures do not cover bills.
feel: I feel **hopeful**, while aware that future paid offers are uncertain.
S4.quote: I also notice how much of my plan depends on a future offer I cannot see today.
fieldNote: Freya’s decade plan relies on **annual pension checks** and a comparison with actual stall earnings.
She would trial an **inspection camera** against what workers find on the pole, while keeping retirement travel secondary to bills.

steps.text: Check pension income against household bills each year
Keep safe repairs and take paid equipment checks if offered
Apply for maintenance work if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I would be only 63 when robots reached the line. A funded course with a real equipment vacancy at the end would help, and so would honest notice about repair shifts. I can learn a new machine; I cannot live on a promise to learn one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I enjoy being the older beginner. Some days I do. I bring a notebook home and work out the fitting I missed, then get it right beside the truck the next morning.

headlineQuote: I can learn a new machine; I cannot live on a promise to learn one.
portrait: Freya is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who likes fault finding but still needs a lead worker to check difficult fittings.
She and partner Nils have about **five months saved**, while his bread stall income varies with weather.
She uses **AI daily** for practice questions and tests answers against a trainer or manual.
Across scenarios, she tests **equipment maintenance** and pension figures while keeping paid repair shifts and asking for actual openings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Freya most because line robots could arrive at 63 while she still needs wages.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded course** linked to an equipment vacancy and honest notice of shift changes would give her choices.
